A flexible branch is pushed into the ground and a string runs from its free end to a resonator in a pit in the earth; the resonator may be a board laid over the pit, or the far end of the string is tied to a stone in the pit. It is played by striking or plucking the string with a stick, and bending the branch changes the tension and the pitch and can make a glissando; the pitch is not stable. It has features of both the harp and the musical bow, and is found in equatorial and southern Africa and in cultures of African origin; the Venda call it kalinga.

The earth harp, also called the ground bow, is a single-string bowed folk chordophone, H-S number 311. A flexible branch is pushed into the ground and a string runs from its free end to a resonator in a pit in the earth; the resonator may be a board laid over the pit, or the far end of the string is tied to a stone in the pit. It is played by striking or plucking the string with a stick, and bending the branch changes the tension and the pitch and can make a glissando; the pitch is not stable. It has features of both the harp and the musical bow, and is found in equatorial and southern Africa and in cultures of African origin; the Venda call it kalinga, the Baka angbindi, and it is also found in Haiti, the Dominican Republic and Cuba. It usually provides a repeated accompaniment to choral songs.
地球豎琴是由美國藝術家威廉·克羅斯（William Close）於1990年代創: The Earth Harp is a contemporary instrument created by the American artist William Close in the 1990s. The innovation grew out of Close's deep interest in architectural acoustics and environmental music. He designed the instrument in order to break past the physical limits of traditional instruments, using the building itself as the resonating chamber. The Earth Harp was first shown in California, and has since been exhibited at festivals and art exhibitions around the world. It stretches extremely long strings between different points on a building, and the resonance of those strings produces a deep and singular timbre; it has been described as a masterpiece that joins architecture, music and environmental art. Its arrival opened a new view of contemporary instrument design, drew the attention of musicians and artists worldwide, and made it an important symbol of experimental music in the twenty-first century.
地球豎琴音色深沉而空靈，具有獨特的環境共鳴特性。其音質介於豎琴與鋼琴之間，帶有溫: The Earth Harp's timbre is deep and ethereal, with a distinctive resonance of place. Its sound lies between the harp and the piano, warm with a faintly desolate quality. The bass is full and powerful, the middle register soft and lovely, the top clear and bright. The instrument uses a building or a natural landform as its resonating body, so that the sound resonates with its surroundings and creates a broad sense of acoustic space. Compared with a traditional harp, the timbre is thicker and blends more readily with the setting; compared with a piano, the resonance lasts longer and the sound flows more. Every string can sound on its own, and the whole effect is like the earth itself singing: natural, vast and full of poetry.
地球豎琴（ground-bow）屬弦鳴樂器，見於赤道非洲、南非及具非洲根源的文化: The earth harp (ground-bow) is a chordophone found in equatorial Africa, southern Africa and cultures of African origin. It is most often heard giving a repeated accompaniment to choral songs: the string is struck or plucked with a stick, and the bow can be bent to change the pitch, producing an unstable, glissando-like sound. In Cuba the instrument appears under the onomatopoeic name tingo-talango; the song Tingo Talango by Julio Cueva is dedicated to it, and Ñico Lora has a song of the same name.
本樂器以一根可彎曲的枝條或去皮幼樹插入地面作弓身，發聲體為單弦，弦的材質未載明。: The instrument uses a flexible branch or a stripped sapling pushed into the ground as its bow, and the sound source is a single string whose material the source does not state. The resonator may be a board laid over a pit, with the string attached to it; other accounts tie the far end of the string to a stone dropped into the pit, the string passing through the board that covers the pit. Apart from the branch, string, board and stone that the source mentions, the materials are not recorded.
演奏時先將具彈性的枝條插入地面，使其自由端經弦連至地面共鳴裝置，常見為坑上覆板，: Begin by pushing a springy branch into the ground and running a string from its free end to the resonator on the ground, usually a board over a pit, with the string attached to the board; alternatively tie the far end to a stone dropped into the pit, with the string passing through the covering board. Sound it by striking with a stick, or by plucking the string in several ways; bending the branch changes the string's tension and pitch. A beginner can practise pulling the branch down, striking it and letting go to get a glissando, though the pitch need not be stable. The instrument is mostly used to give a repeated accompaniment to choral songs, so the aim is to keep the rhythm and control the tension rather than to hold a fixed pitch.
